analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from using age to cut older workers' benefits and sets strict rules before they can get workers to waive age-discrimination claims.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the Senate 94-1 and the House 406-17 and became Public Law 101-433 on October 16, 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1989 the Supreme Court ruled that federal age discrimination law did not apply to employee benefits like pensions, health insurance, and disability pay. This bill reversed that by law: employers generally cannot pay less toward an older worker's benefits than a younger worker's, unless a real cost difference justifies it. It also stopped employers from getting older workers to sign away their age-discrimination rights without clear, knowing agreement, with extra protections when a whole group of employees is being offered buyouts.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers age 40 and over, and especially those near retirement. After the Supreme Court's 1989 Betts decision, employers could legally cut their health, disability, and pension benefits based on age; this law restores the ban, requires employers to prove their benefit plans and early retirement arrangements are lawful, and stops companies from using fine-print release agreements to make workers give up age-discrimination claims when taking severance or buyouts.

how_it_helps.text: Restores protection against age discrimination in all employee benefits, including health, life, disability, and pension benefits, which the Supreme Court's Betts decision had excluded.

Requires employers to spend no less on an older worker's benefit than on a younger worker's, per benefit or benefit package, unless an age-based reduction is justified by significant cost considerations.

Makes an employee's waiver of age discrimination claims unenforceable unless it is knowing and voluntary, with minimum standards including required consideration periods and extra safeguards when waivers are offered to a group of employees facing layoffs or exit incentives.
Places the burden on the employer to prove that challenged actions or waivers are lawful, rather than on the older worker to prove they are not.
Applies the protections to cases pending or filed after June 23, 1989, the day the Supreme Court decided Betts, so workers whose cases were already in court were not left without a remedy.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, which must either pay equal benefits for older workers or prove any age-based differences reflect genuine cost considerations, and which face new requirements before they can obtain waivers of age claims in severance agreements. Government employers and pension plan sponsors get a phase-in period to adjust.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts certain long-standing defined benefit pension plan practices and specific benefit-coordination arrangements from the equal-benefit rule, so some age-based differences in those plans remain lawful.
The cost-basis exception still lets employers pay less toward older workers' benefits where genuine cost differences can be shown, which limits the guarantee of equal value.

Under collective bargaining agreements, the new rules do not apply until the agreement ends or June 1, 1992, whichever is first, delaying relief for some union-represented workers, and state and local government benefit plans get a two-year phase-in.

Employers bear the cost of proving that benefit plan and early retirement arrangements are lawful, and equal-cost requirements can make certain benefits for older workers more expensive to maintain or offer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to older workers are concrete and directly reverse a Supreme Court decision that had stripped their protection; the main costs fall on employers and plan administrators in the form of higher benefit spending and heavier legal burdens. The carve-outs for existing pension plan features, coordination with disability benefits, and union contracts until mid-1992 soften the bill's bite and add complexity, but the core equal-benefit principle and the waiver protections are strong. For ordinary workers this was a clear net win.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 94-1, the House passed it 406-17 under a fast-tracked procedure that needed two-thirds, and the President signed it into law in October 1990.

narrative.text: The bill responded to the Supreme Court's 1989 Betts decision, which had held that the age discrimination law generally did not cover employee benefit plans.
The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee reported the bill favorably on April 5, 1990, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute and a written report.
The Senate passed the amended bill on September 24, 1990, by a vote of 94 to 1.
The House passed the Senate bill on October 3, 1990, 406 to 17, under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure that required a two-thirds majority.
The President signed it on October 16, 1990, and it became Public Law 101-433.
As enacted, the bill restored equal-benefit protections, preserved some early retirement incentives, and added new standards for waiver of age discrimination claims.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Older workers came out ahead: their anti-discrimination protections in benefits were restored, and severance waivers can no longer be used to quietly take away their legal claims. Employers that had relied on Betts to cut benefits by age bear the new costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Older workers; employers lost a loophole

sides.party_line_note: The vote was overwhelmingly bipartisan: the Senate passed it 94-1 with 53 of 55 Democrats and 41 of 45 Republicans in favor, and the House passed it 406-17, with all 17 no votes coming from Republicans.

industries.industry: Employers with benefit plans and early retirement programs
industries.note: Employers can no longer cut benefits based on age except for documented cost reasons, must prove their plans comply, and face stricter rules before severance deals can waive age claims. This raises their benefit costs and legal exposure.

The bill subjects pension benefits to anti-discrimination rules but exempts certain long-standing plan features and allows disability benefits to be offset by pension benefits in defined circumstances, so some age-based practices are preserved.
Unions gain from a fairer burden of proof in enforcement cases, but existing collective bargaining agreements are shielded from the new rules until they expire or June 1, 1992.
Their employee benefit plans must eventually comply, but the law gives them a two-year delay and lets them offer existing employees a choice between old and new disability benefits.
